claims.text: As-received Q235 steel bears a naturally formed native oxide film.
The corrosion behavior of as-received Q235 steel is governed by the integrity of its surface oxide film.
At room temperature, the native oxide film on Q235 steel is thin, compact, and continuous.
The native oxide film passivates Q235 steel at room temperature.
At 750–850 °C under a NaCl deposit, thermal stresses and salt fluxing cause the oxide film to crack and spall.
High-temperature exposure causes phase transformations and microcrack development in the oxide.
Oxide cracking and spallation expose fresh metal and thereby accelerate corrosion.
The oxide scale is primarily composed of Fe2O3 and Fe3O4.
Controlled pre-oxidation changes oxide thickness, continuity, phase composition, and adhesion.
Optimized pre-oxidation produces a thicker, more uniform, and more adherent oxide film than is present on untreated specimens.
A pre-oxidized oxide layer better resists thermally induced cracking.
Pre-oxidation delays or reduces high-temperature corrosion relative to untreated Q235 steel.
At room temperature, both untreated and pre-oxidized specimens will exhibit effective corrosion resistance because their oxide films remain stable.
At high temperature, untreated specimens will exhibit more oxide cracking and spallation than pre-oxidized specimens.
At high temperature, untreated specimens will suffer more corrosion than pre-oxidized specimens.
Aggressive corrosion initiates only after detectable thermally induced disruption of the oxide film.
A robust, adherent oxide layer will correlate with delayed or reduced corrosion damage.
The proposed mechanism may not apply when different salt chemistries or nonthermal mechanical stresses dominate corrosion.
